content.text: why do we have system agent, what's the point? in a world we support all external agents and managed agents are optional, do you think we need to auto providionn ti

I don’t think we should auto-provision it.

Today the “system agent” is really an optional managed **workspace operator**:

- It gets privileged management tools only when an owner/admin is speaking to it ([message-consumer.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/orchestration/message-consumer.ts:71)).
- It powers Builder chat, chat-driven agent creation, the workspace landing page, and Slack onboarding.
- External MCP agents already access management capabilities through user role × OAuth scope; they do not need a system agent ([execute.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/tools/execute.ts:126)).

So I would keep the nullable role/pointer because it is a useful security chokepoint for managed agents, but change the invariant to:

> A Lobu workspace is fully functional with `system_agent_id = NULL`.

Then:

- Stop provisioning Builder during signup.
- Make `GET /system-agent` read-only; it currently creates/heals one merely by loading the UI ([agent-routes.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/lobu/agent-routes.ts:346)).
- Provision only when the user explicitly chooses **Enable Builder**, starts managed chat, or opts into Builder during Slack onboarding.
- If no Builder exists, land on a neutral workspace/activity view with “Connect an external agent” and “Enable Builder.”
- Support clearing the pointer; currently it can be reassigned but not unset.
- Preserve existing Builders—just stop creating new ones implicitly.

The current approach conflates “Lobu supports managed agents” with “every workspace must own one.” It also creates unused agent rows and inference-model obligations; we have already seen auto-provisioned Builders left unrunnable with missing model configuration.

Product-facing, I’d avoid “system agent” entirely. Call it **Builder** or **workspace operator**. Internally, `system_agent_id` can remain until a deliberate schema redesign.

No code was changed; I verified this against freshly fetched `origin/main` at `a439bc346`.

figure out where this system agent is being used and let's see if we can fully get rid of it. instead. when there is zero agent in a workspace we can just show connect your agent and build a managed agent section

Yes—we can fully remove the system-agent runtime concept. It is not foundational to external agents or ordinary managed agents.

## Where it is used today

| Area | Current purpose | Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| Provisioning | Creates `lobu-builder` during signup, local bootstrap, Slack claim, and even `GET /system-agent` ([builder-provisioning.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/auth/builder-provisioning.ts)) | Delete provisioning; agents exist only through explicit create/apply |
| Authorization | Lets every owner/admin use one shared agent and supplies a per-turn workspace-admin tool allowlist ([message-consumer.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/orchestration/message-consumer.ts)) | Remove the special managed-admin path; UI/session and external OAuth retain normal role × scope authorization |
| Agent API | Special owner/admin access instead of ordinary agent ownership ([agent.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent.ts)) | All managed agents follow the normal ownership/permissions model |
| MCP/SDK | Exposes `set_system_agent` and `is_system_agent` ([manage-agents.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/core/src/contracts/tools/manage-agents.ts)) | Remove both from the public contract and generated SDK |
| Slack | Creates Builder and binds the installer’s DM to it ([slack-claim-onboarding.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/connections/slack-claim-onboarding.ts)) | Install the connection, then ask the user to choose/build a managed agent before binding |
| Owletto home | Redirects workspace home into Builder chat ([owner route](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/owletto/src/app/$owner.tsx)) | Make workspace home a neutral surface |
| Agent creation | “New agent” is a prompt sent to Builder | Open an explicit managed-agent creation form |
| Activity | Workspace-wide attention is embedded below Builder chat | Move it onto workspace home |
| Database | `organization.system_agent_id` plus provisioning sentinel | Stop reads/writes, then drop the column in a later rollout |

The `codex-skills/lobu-builder` package is unrelated—it is a coding skill for building Lobu projects and should remain. Historical migrations and changelog entries should also remain as history.

## Proposed zero-agent home

When there are no managed agents:

- **Connect your agent**
  - ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Codex, or another MCP client.
  - Reuse the existing MCP-client setup and connected-app infrastructure.

- **Build a managed agent**
  - Open the existing agent creation form.
  - Require or guide model/provider setup so we do not create another unrunnable row.
  - After creation, route to the agent’s Desk/configuration.

Workspace home should remain neutral even after agents exist: workspace attention, connected external agents, and managed agents. It should not arbitrarily redirect to the first agent.

## One adjacent path must also go

There is a second auto-provisioned managed agent: `owletto-default`, plus its daily Behavior ([default-provisioning.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/auth/default-provisioning.ts)). Signup and local `lobu run` currently create it.

If managed agents are genuinely optional, I recommend removing this too. That also means:

- Stop implicit `owletto-default` creation.
- Stop automatic daily-Behavior creation.
- Require an explicit `agentId` when starting managed chat instead of silently choosing `owletto-default`.
- Keep `lobu apply` and explicit UI creation as valid ways to create managed agents.

Otherwise, fresh workspaces would still usually never reach the zero-agent experience.

## Existing production Builders

Do not bulk-delete them. Existing `lobu-builder` rows may own conversations and Slack bindings.

Instead:

- Preserve them as ordinary managed agents.
- Remove their special privileges/designation.
- Let their existing bindings and history continue working.
- Make them normally deletable.
- Drop only the pointer; users can decide whether to keep or delete the legacy agent.

## Rollout shape

This needs two releases for rolling-deploy safety:

1. Ship the neutral Owletto home, zero-agent onboarding, explicit managed creation, stop all auto-provisioning and special authorization, and make `/system-agent` non-mutating.
2. After that version is fully deployed, remove `/system-agent`, `set_system_agent`, `is_system_agent`, generated SDK methods, and drop `organization.system_agent_id`.

This is a database and public API/SDK contract change, so I have not started editing. Please confirm that the intended scope includes removing both `lobu-builder` and the `owletto-default`/daily-Behavior auto-provisioning; that is the version I recommend.

why defauly behavior isn't it confusing?

Yes, the default daily Behavior is confusing.

It was originally added for Mac onboarding so a fresh install demonstrated value immediately: create `owletto-default`, then schedule a 9am daily check-in on the first paired device. But it silently assumes the user wants:

- A Lobu-managed personal assistant
- A daily summary
- A 9am schedule
- Device-local execution
- A configured model and enough data to produce something useful

Those are product choices, not safe defaults.

In the external-agent-first model, a new workspace should contain:

- Zero managed agents
- Zero Behaviors
- Connected external agents only when authorized

“Daily check-in” can remain as an optional starter template shown after someone creates a managed agent and connects a device. It should be explicitly selected, never auto-provisioned.
yes no need for that but don't we support behaviors for the external agents?

Yes—but current support is only half-complete.

External MCP agents can already create, inspect, update, and trigger Behaviors through `manage_behaviors`. However, execution still requires a Lobu-managed agent:

- Behavior creation requires `agent_id`.
- That ID must exist in the `agents` table ([crud.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/tools/admin/manage_behaviors/crud.ts)).
- Scheduled/manual runs dispatch that assigned Lobu agent ([automation.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/watchers/automation.ts)).

There is a `scheduler_client_id` field described as an MCP client that should auto-run the Behavior, but on current `origin/main` it is only stored and returned—no scheduler or dispatcher actually consumes it. So ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, etc. cannot currently be awakened by Lobu.

The correct model is:

- Behavior belongs to the workspace.
- Its author may be a human, external agent, or managed agent.
- Its executor is explicit:
  - Managed Lobu agent
  - Durable external runner that polls/subscribes for work
  - None yet, meaning draft/inactive
- A normal MCP client can author and interactively trigger Behaviors, but Lobu cannot push work into it unless that client implements a durable callback/polling protocol.

So we should remove the default/system agents without removing Behaviors. But to support Behaviors in a zero-managed-agent workspace honestly, we need to decouple Behavior ownership from `agent_id` and finish the external-executor contract. We should not silently create a managed agent merely to satisfy the current execution model.

No code changed; this was verified against current `origin/main`.

Yes — I’d separate these concepts cleanly:

| Concept | Examples | Where it belongs |
|---|---|---|
| Agent | ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, managed Lobu agent | **Agents** |
| Access client/device | Lobu CLI, Chrome extension, Mac app | Settings → Connected apps/devices |
| Behavior | Workspace automation definition | Top-level **Behaviors** |

The current sidebar is confusing because it renders every connected `kind: "mcp"` client as an agent. The server actually considers those OAuth registrations “Connected Apps”; the UI is grouping by transport rather than meaning. See [client-routes.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/lobu/client-routes.ts) and [app-sidebar.tsx](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/owletto/src/components/sidebar/app-sidebar.tsx).

For the CLI specifically: we should not try to infer the agent. “Lobu CLI” could mean a human terminal, Codex, Claude, CI, or a script. Even the current `drivenBy` value only identifies the process driving MCP, not a trustworthy agent identity.

The rule should be:

- A CLI session remains attributed as “via Lobu CLI.”
- If Codex or another external agent wants to appear under Agents, it explicitly declares an agent identity.
- No user-agent or process-name guessing.
- Directly connected ChatGPT/Claude/custom-agent integrations declare `role: agent`; CLI, Chrome and Mac declare `role: tool` or `device`.

I also agree Behaviors should move out of individual agents into a top-level workspace section. The current route structure makes every Behavior look managed-agent-owned, even though external agents can author and manage them.

For execution, I’d use this model:

- Each trigger may optionally name a managed executor.
- With an executor: Lobu dispatches the run automatically.
- Without one: Lobu creates an **available Behavior run**.
- Authorized external agents can list, atomically claim, process and complete available runs through MCP.
- If nobody claims it, it remains pending; Lobu does not silently provision or fall back to a system agent.

That last part requires a real durable work-inbox/claim contract. MCP clients cannot be pushed awake, and allowing several clients to “process if they want” without an atomic claim would cause duplicate execution. Existing run infrastructure has durable claim machinery, but there is not currently a public external-agent Behavior claim flow.

So my recommended direction is:

1. Agents sidebar contains only explicitly declared reasoning agents.
2. CLI/Chrome/Mac disappear from that list but remain manageable as connected clients/devices.
3. Behaviors becomes top-level and workspace-owned.
4. Remove required Behavior `agent_id`; execution is configured per trigger.
5. Unassigned triggers produce claimable work for external agents.
6. Zero-agent workspace shows “Connect your agent” plus an optional “Build a managed agent” section.

This changes the Behavior and client contracts, so I’d want your explicit confirmation on that shape before implementing it.

so on cli for example how would we do this properly. or should we show those under connectors instead and only show the known agents in the sidebar and the mcp client vendors

For the CLI, the proper behavior is: **the CLI is never an agent by itself**.

Three cases:

| Usage | Identity shown |
|---|---|
| Human runs `lobu` | “Via Lobu CLI” in Activity |
| Codex uses a shared/general CLI login | Still “Via Lobu CLI”; don’t guess Codex |
| Codex connects using its own agent profile/token | Codex appears under Agents; Activity says “Codex via Lobu CLI” |

To support the third case properly, the CLI could use explicit profiles:

```bash
lobu login --profile codex --agent
lobu behavior runs claim --profile codex
```

That login would create or link a server-issued external-agent identity. Claims would record both:

- `agent_id`: the external Codex identity
- `client_id`: the Lobu CLI OAuth registration used for access

I would not place CLI and Chrome directly under **Connectors** either. GitHub, Gmail and Slack are connectors; CLI and Chrome are clients/devices that provide access. Putting them together creates another category problem.

My preferred navigation:

- **Agents**
  - Managed Lobu agents
  - Known agent products: ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Cursor, etc.
  - Custom clients that explicitly register themselves as `role: agent`

- **Behaviors**
  - Workspace-level Behavior definitions and available work

- **Connectors**
  - GitHub, Gmail, Slack, browser, databases, and other capabilities/data sources

- **Settings → Clients & devices**
  - Lobu CLI registrations
  - Chrome extension
  - Mac app
  - OAuth grants, tokens, last activity and revocation

Known vendor recognition can provide trusted names and icons, but it shouldn’t be the only way into Agents. Unknown clients should remain under Clients & devices unless they explicitly register as an agent. We should never classify something as an agent just because its MCP client name contains “Claude” or “Codex.”

So the central distinction is:

> **Agent = who performs the work. Client = how they access Lobu. Connector = what capability or data they use.**

That also gives us accurate attribution like “Codex via Lobu CLI used GitHub,” without pretending that the CLI or GitHub is the agent.
why don't we show the mac app chrome extension etc under connectors?

We can—and I think that is probably the cleaner product.

“Connectors” can mean **everything connecting the workspace to an external client, device, service, or capability**, with sections distinguishing their roles:

- **Services:** GitHub, Gmail, Slack, databases
- **Devices and runtimes:** Chrome extension, Mac app
- **Developer clients:** Lobu CLI
- **Other MCP clients:** unknown or tool-oriented MCP registrations

Then **Agents** remains narrowly about who performs work:

- Managed Lobu agents
- ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and other known agent vendors
- Custom MCP clients explicitly declaring themselves as agents

The important part is that the Connector cards should explain their function:

- “Chrome Extension — provides browser access”
- “Mac App — hosts local connectors”
- “Lobu CLI — command-line access”
- “GitHub — provides repository data and actions”

An agent could still have a detail link saying “Connected through Lobu CLI,” but the CLI itself wouldn’t occupy an Agents row.

So yes: move Mac, Chrome, CLI and non-agent MCP clients under Connectors. Use explicit agent classification—not merely `kind: "mcp"`—to decide what also appears in Agents. This gives us one understandable rule:

> Agents do work. Connectors give agents and people access to Lobu or the outside world.
ok sounds good. can you identify all the gaps here

The direction is sound, but this is not just a sidebar cleanup. Four concepts are currently collapsed together:

| Concept | Should represent |
|---|---|
| Agents | Reasoning actors: managed or external |
| Connectors | Apps, devices, OAuth grants, CLI transports |
| Behaviors | Workspace-owned jobs |
| Runs | Durable execution claimed by an eligible actor |

Fresh `origin/main` does not yet have the identity or execution contracts needed to keep those separate.

## 1. Agent versus MCP-client classification

The new Owletto change puts every connected MCP registration under Agents. The server only exposes `kind: "mcp"`; it does not say whether the client is an agent, device, CLI, extension, or other tool.

Gaps:

- Add a semantic role such as `agent_host`, `connector_client`, `device_app`, or `tooling`.
- Unknown clients should default to Connector-only.
- Custom external agents need an explicit declaration/registration path.
- Client names and `software_id` are self-asserted through dynamic registration. Matching “Claude” or “ChatGPT” is useful presentation logic, not trusted identity.
- `clientInfo.name` identifies the process driving MCP, not the app or agent.
- One OAuth registration may serve multiple agents, humans, CI jobs, or profiles.
- “Connected” currently means an active OAuth token exists, not that an agent is online.
- We need distinct states: authorized, recently active, currently online, disconnected, revoked.
- Known agent hosts can intentionally appear twice:
  - Agents: actor/inbox/activity
  - Connectors: grant, scopes, registrations, revoke

The current raw registration projection is in [client-routes.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/lobu/client-routes.ts:205).

## 2. External-agent identity does not exist

Today:

- `agents` represents configured Lobu-managed agents.
- `oauth_clients` represents application grants.
- MCP sessions can optionally bind to an existing managed `agent_id`.
- There is no persistent external-agent profile.

This blocks reliable roster membership, Behavior assignment, claim provenance, and multiple agents behind Lobu CLI.

A design decision is required before implementation:

- Extend `agents` into a common actor table with managed/external kinds; or
- Add external-agent profiles and expose a unified roster projection.

I lean toward a common agent identity with managed configuration stored separately, but that is a schema/API decision that should be explicitly approved first.

## 3. Lobu CLI is a transport, not an agent

The CLI always registers as `Lobu CLI`/`lobu-cli`. The server cannot tell whether the caller is Codex, Claude, a human shell, CI, or a custom agent.

Therefore:

- Lobu CLI belongs under Connectors by default.
- An agent using the CLI needs to declare a separate stable agent profile/identity.
- Every call/run should preserve both:
  - actor: “Codex on Burak’s Mac”
  - transport: “via Lobu CLI”
- Reusing one CLI credential across several actors must not merge them into one agent.
- Older CLI clients without actor metadata should remain Connector-only.

The same installation-versus-actor distinction applies to the Mac app and Chrome extension.

## 4. Behaviors are still structurally owned by managed agents

Although the backend can list Behaviors workspace-wide, creation requires `agent_id`, and scheduling/activation explicitly excludes Behaviors without one:

- [Behavior creation](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/tools/admin/manage_behaviors/crud.ts:111)
- [Event activation](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/behaviors/activation.ts:115)
- [Scheduled activation](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/watchers/automation.ts:736)

Other coupling includes:

- `watchers.agent_id` is `NOT NULL`.
- Routes and deep links live below `/agents/:agentId/behaviors`.
- Authorization is inherited through the owning agent.
- Skills must be enabled in the owning agent’s library.
- Model selection falls back to the owning agent.
- Execution permissions, guardrails, identity and persona come from that agent.
- UI creation always preselects an agent.
- Empty states describe Behaviors as making “this agent” act.

Moving Behaviors top-level therefore requires a real ownership and authorization change, not only new navigation.

## 5. Optional agent per trigger needs a new trigger contract

Triggers currently answer only “when.” Executor selection is Behavior-level.

Missing decisions and mechanics:

- Stable trigger IDs. Array position is not durable enough for routing.
- A discriminated executor, likely along the lines of:
  - managed agent
  - named external agent
  - any eligible external agent
  - pinned device
- A Behavior-level default for manual runs, because they have no trigger.
- Whether model, skills, guardrails and delivery are per Behavior or per executor.
- Whether an external agent treats skills/model configuration as requirements, hints, or irrelevant managed-only configuration.
- What happens when several event triggers match; today the first match wins.
- Existing run uniqueness is per Behavior, not per trigger. The database allows only one executing run and one pending non-event run per Behavior. Different trigger/executor lanes would currently block one another. See [the run indexes](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/db/migrations/20260720140000_rename_run_type_watcher_to_behavior.sql:65).
- Runs need to snapshot stable trigger identity and chosen executor for auditability.

This is probably the most consequential hidden schema change.

## 6. `scheduler_client_id` is dead configuration

The field is exposed in the contract, persisted, versioned, edited in Owletto and included in SDK output, but there is no runtime consumer that dispatches work to it.

Worse, the UI queries clients through an agent-filtered endpoint that deliberately excludes generic MCP registrations, so it can present messaging identities as “Runs on.”

It should be removed or replaced by the new executor contract, not expanded.

## 7. There is no external Behavior claim protocol

The durable `runs` table already has useful atomic claiming, heartbeat and claimant fencing. However, public MCP clients cannot:

- List available Behavior runs.
- Atomically claim one.
- Renew a lease.
- Release/defer it.
- Submit a result with claimant fencing.
- Reconcile an ambiguous completion.
- Advertise capabilities used for eligibility.

Additional decisions:

- Who can claim: any member, admins, an allowlist, or only an assigned external agent?
- How long unclaimed runs remain available.
- Retry and dead-letter semantics.
- Whether external agents poll—the server cannot wake an arbitrary MCP client.
- How `turn` executions return an answer.
- Whether `reply_to_source` is supported when the claimant does not own the source transport.
- How approval and connector authorization are enforced without granting the claimant managed-worker authority.
- How claim identity binds agent profile, OAuth `client_id`, user and organization.

Existing `complete_window` is useful but insufficient because it does not establish that the submitting client owns the claimed run.

## 8. System Builder removal touches many workflows

The system agent is not isolated provisioning code. It currently provides:

- Personal-organization Builder creation.
- Local/bootstrap Builder creation.
- Slack claim onboarding.
- A mutating `GET /agents/system-agent` recovery path.
- Owner-home redirect.
- “New agent” through a Builder prompt.
- Command-palette “Ask the builder.”
- Special system-agent authorization and history resolution.
- Special per-turn administrative tool grants.
- `manage_agents.set_system_agent`, `is_system_agent`, deletion protection.
- `organization.system_agent_id`.

The main provisioning entry is [builder-provisioning.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/auth/builder-provisioning.ts:151).

Removal needs to:

- Stop all automatic provisioning and read-time healing.
- Replace owner home with a real workspace landing/zero state.
- Add direct managed-agent creation instead of prompting Builder.
- Replace the Builder’s implicit admin delegation.
- Retire the pointer/API/public contract in stages.
- Preserve existing Builder rows as ordinary managed agents; do not delete them.

## 9. There is a second default agent and default Behavior

Separate from Builder, `ensureDefaultAgent` creates `owletto-default`, and device polling can automatically create a daily Behavior.

Relevant paths:

- [default-provisioning.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/auth/default-provisioning.ts:227)
- [worker poll](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/worker-api/poll.ts:325)

For truly optional managed agents:

- Signup/bootstrap must no longer create the default.
- Agent-less API calls cannot silently resolve to it.
- Device pairing must not create a daily Behavior.
- Local/self-hosted CLI assumptions need explicit configuration.
- Existing default agents and Behaviors must remain untouched.
- A workspace without a model provider must still be valid until someone builds a managed agent.

## 10. Navigation and zero-state gaps

Behaviors moving top-level requires:

- `/behaviors`, `/behaviors/new`, `/behaviors/:id`.
- Top-level sidebar and collapsed-rail entries.
- Rewriting server-generated URLs, notifications, Activity cards, approvals, Recent links and command-palette results.
- Redirects from legacy agent-scoped Behavior URLs.
- Deciding whether agent pages retain a filtered “Behaviors using this agent” shortcut.
- External-agent row destinations—Connector details alone may not be enough.

The zero-agent workspace should offer two equal paths:

- Connect your agent.
- Build a managed agent.

Connectors should continue showing Mac, Chrome, Lobu CLI, MCP grants and devices. It also needs to avoid confusing duplication when one installation appears both as a device worker and an OAuth registration.

## 11. Migration and compatibility gaps

A safe migration needs to cover:

- Convert every existing `agent_id` into the equivalent managed executor assignment without changing scheduling.
- Assign stable IDs to existing triggers.
- Preserve device-pinned behavior.
- Remove or translate `scheduler_client_id`.
- Default historical OAuth clients to Connector-only.
- Preserve existing Builder/default agents as ordinary managed agents.
- Update Core contracts, generated ClientSDK types, CLI apply/diff/config, docs and skill text.
- Keep compatibility redirects for old Behavior links.
- Release Owletto first, then update the parent submodule pointer.

## 12. Required verification

The critical new tests are:

- Mac, Chrome and Lobu CLI never appear as agents merely because they connected.
- Known and explicitly declared external agents do appear.
- Unknown/spoofed registrations remain Connector-only.
- Zero-agent signup and device pairing create no hidden agent or Behavior.
- Legacy Behaviors retain identical schedule/event/manual/device behavior.
- Multi-replica claim races produce exactly one external claimant.
- Heartbeat expiry, reclaim, duplicate completion and stale claimant fencing.
- Per-trigger execution and global-versus-trigger run concurrency.
- Authorization cannot escalate through claiming.
- All old and new deep links resolve.

My recommended order is:

1. Approve the actor/client classification and external-agent identity model.
2. Ship the sidebar/Connectors classification and zero-agent landing.
3. Approve the per-trigger executor and external claim contracts.
4. Migrate Behaviors top-level.
5. Stop provisioning system/default agents.
6. Retire legacy pointers and contracts after compatibility telemetry.

do you think behaviors should move out of agents?

Yes—Behaviors should move out of agent ownership, but agents should still expose their relationship to them.

A Behavior is fundamentally a workspace job:

- Trigger: when it runs.
- Instructions and sources: what it does.
- Executor: who processes this particular trigger or run.

The executor can be a managed agent, a named external agent, any eligible external agent, or a device. That makes the agent a replaceable execution choice, not the Behavior’s natural container.

I’d make `/behaviors` the canonical top-level surface, while each agent page retains an “Assigned Behaviors” view linking back to those Behaviors.

For example:

- Behavior: “Process new support tickets”
- Email trigger → managed Support Agent
- Slack trigger → external Claude agent
- Manual run → choose an agent at run time
- Unassigned trigger → available for eligible MCP agents to claim

The important caveat is sequencing: moving only the UI would be misleading because Behaviors are still deeply agent-owned in the database, authorization, skills, models, URLs and dispatcher. First introduce the executor contract and workspace ownership; then move the navigation.

So my recommendation is: **move Behaviors out of Agents as the canonical home, while keeping agent-scoped filtered views as useful shortcuts.**

content.text:
I audited this workstream against fresh `origin/main` (`a985a204`) and its pinned Owletto commit (`5ea8dea`). The clean architecture is:

- Agents are durable actors.
- Connectors are applications, devices, transports and OAuth grants.
- An actor may use one or more connectors.
- Every action preserves both actor identity and transport identity.

The current system has only managed-agent identity and connected-client identity. It has no durable external-agent identity between them.

## Current correctness gaps

- Every OAuth/MCP registration is returned as `kind: "mcp"` from `client-routes.ts`.
- Owletto groups every connected MCP client and places it under Agents.
- Mac, Chrome, Lobu CLI and generic MCP clients already belong to—and appear under—Connectors.
- `client_name`, `software_id`, redirect URIs and MCP `clientInfo` are self-asserted. The unauthenticated DCR endpoint cannot establish a trusted vendor or actor.
- `clientInfo.name` identifies the process driving MCP, not the app or actor.
- One OAuth registration can have grants for multiple users.
- One CLI credential can be used by a human, Codex, Claude or CI.
- The current registration group key is suitable for Connector display/revocation only. It is not a durable actor identifier.
- An active OAuth token is currently rendered as “connected,” even when no process is online.
- Existing MCP `agentId` binding means “scope this session to an existing managed Lobu agent.” Reusing it for an external actor would mix two different security models.
- Activity records the OAuth `client_id`, but has no separate external actor identity.
- The sidebar’s current CLI exclusion is a one-off `software_id = lobu-cli` filter rather than a semantic client classification.

## Recommended identity model

Do not turn every OAuth client into an agent, and do not overload the current `agents` table immediately.

The least risky model is:

1. Keep `agents` as managed Lobu agent configurations.
2. Add a durable external-agent profile.
3. Bind external profiles to authenticated OAuth grants/transports.
4. Expose a unified roster projection for the UI.

Conceptually:

```text
Managed agent ─────┐
                   ├── Agent roster
External profile ──┘
       │
       ├── OAuth grant via ChatGPT
       ├── OAuth grant via Lobu CLI
       └── MCP session via another client
```

An external profile should carry stable identity, display name, vendor hint, lifecycle state, capabilities and workspace ownership. Its transport binding must include organization, OAuth client and authorizing user because one client registration can be shared by multiple users.

I recommend a separate external profile initially because virtually every consumer of `agents` currently assumes models, skills, permissions, prompts and managed-worker execution. Adding external rows there would make those assumptions conditionally unsafe across the whole codebase. A future parent actor table can unify storage after the semantics settle.

## Approval decisions

These should be explicitly settled before schema or API implementation:

1. **Roster unit**

   Recommended: a stable actor profile, not a client vendor or OAuth registration.

2. **Profile storage**

   Recommended: separate external-agent profiles plus grant bindings; leave managed `agents` unchanged.

3. **Who may create one**

   Recommended: members may register an external agent acting with their own grant; owners/admins decide whether it may be workspace-assigned or claim Behaviors.

4. **Known-vendor meaning**

   Recommended: vendor-name recognition is cosmetic unless backed by a signed software statement, pre-registered client, or workspace confirmation. Never use a name match for authorization.

5. **Existing ChatGPT/Claude grants**

   Options are:
   - Show them only under Connectors until the next authenticated actor declaration.
   - Create an explicitly “recognized, unverified” profile lazily on next use.
   - Prompt the member/admin to convert the grant into an external agent.

   I recommend lazy recognition plus an unverified label, with Behavior eligibility disabled until actor capability is declared.

6. **CLI actor UX**

   We need to choose whether actor selection is:
   - Per invocation/environment.
   - A named CLI profile.
   - A separate CLI context.

   Recommended: a named actor profile selected per process/invocation. The existing context remains an endpoint/login context.

7. **Presence semantics**

   Recommended:
   - Authorized: live OAuth grant exists.
   - Online: a durable, unexpired MCP presence lease exists.
   - Last active: materialized write-time timestamp.
   - Offline: authorized but no live lease.
   - Revoked: no usable grant.

8. **External-agent detail destination**

   Recommended: an external-agent detail page, not a chat page. Show chat only if a future capability supports inbound Lobu conversations.

## Dependency-aware implementation plan

### Phase 0: Correct the current sidebar

This phase is independent of the new identity design and can ship immediately.

- Remove raw `connectedAppGroups` from the Agents sidebar.
- Leave every OAuth/MCP registration in Connectors.
- Keep managed agents in Agents.
- Do not infer agent status from an OAuth token.
- When the managed roster is empty, render:
  - Connect your agent.
  - Build a managed agent.

Likely Owletto ownership:

- `src/components/sidebar/app-sidebar.tsx`
- `src/components/sidebar/app-sidebar.test.tsx`
- `src/lib/connectors/client-rows.ts`
- Connector list/detail tests as regression coverage

Acceptance:

- Mac, Chrome, Lobu CLI, generic MCP and unknown applications never appear under Agents.
- They remain visible and revocable under Connectors.
- The zero-agent state is useful rather than blank.
- No server or schema dependency.

### Phase 1: Freeze the shared contracts

Add two separate DTO families:

- Connector/grant inventory.
- Agent roster.

The Connector DTO should expose semantic presentation information without treating it as actor identity:

```ts
type ClientPresentationKind =
  | "cli"
  | "desktop_app"
  | "browser_extension"
  | "agent_host"
  | "generic_mcp"
  | "unknown";

type ClassificationSource =
  | "verified"
  | "workspace_declared"
  | "catalog_hint"
  | "unclassified";
```

The roster should be discriminated:

```ts
type AgentRosterItem =
  | {
      kind: "managed";
      agentId: string;
      status: "active" | "idle";
      // managed configuration summary
    }
  | {
      kind: "external";
      agentId: string;
      vendor?: string;
      trust: "verified" | "workspace_declared" | "recognized";
      availability: "online" | "offline";
      authState: "authorized" | "revoked";
      capabilities: string[];
      connectedVia: ClientReference[];
    };
```

Keep `GET /api/:org/agents` managed-only because CLI apply, configuration and current agent tooling depend on that meaning. Add a roster endpoint such as `GET /api/:org/agents/roster`.

Likely ownership:

- `packages/core/src/contracts/` for canonical DTO/schema
- `packages/server/src/lobu/agent-routes.ts` or a dedicated roster route
- `packages/server/src/lobu/client-routes.ts`
- `packages/server/src/index.ts`
- Contract and route tests
- Owletto client API types only after the contract freezes

Acceptance:

- The server, not UI substring matching, supplies classification.
- A DTO never calls an OAuth grant an agent.
- Managed configuration endpoints remain backward compatible.
- Old clients ignore additive fields safely.

### Phase 2: Add durable external-agent profiles

After schema approval, add:

- External-agent profile storage.
- Profile-to-grant binding storage.
- Indexed, write-time lifecycle and last-activity fields.
- Create/update/archive/bind operations.
- No hard deletion of profiles referenced by audit records.

Important binding dimensions:

- `organization_id`
- external profile ID
- OAuth `client_id`
- authorizing `user_id`
- lifecycle state
- declaration/trust source

Do not create organization profiles during unauthenticated DCR. DCR may record an untrusted hint, but profile creation/binding occurs only after authentication or explicit workspace action.

Do not use `client_name + owner + org` as a foreign identity key. Re-registration must be handled through an explicit binding/recovery flow.

Likely ownership:

- New migration in `db/migrations/`
- New server store under `packages/server/src/lobu/stores/`
- New or extended route module under `packages/server/src/lobu/`
- `packages/core` contract
- Route/store/integration tests

Acceptance:

- Profiles are stable across reconnects and client re-registration.
- Shared OAuth registrations remain isolated by user grant.
- Archiving a profile preserves historical attribution.
- Creating a profile grants no additional OAuth scope or member role.
- All reads remain bounded/config-table reads; no history aggregation.

### Phase 3: Separate MCP actor binding from managed-agent binding

Introduce a distinct external actor declaration during authenticated MCP initialization.

Do not reuse:

- `requested_agent_id`
- `x-lobu-agent-id`
- `ToolContext.agentId`

Those currently bind to a managed agent and select managed-agent authorization behavior.

Instead add a separate identity such as:

- `requestedExternalAgentId`
- `externalAgentId`
- a separately named initialization metadata field/header

The server must verify:

- Profile belongs to the current organization.
- Current user/client grant is bound to it.
- Profile is active.
- The declared capabilities are allowed.
- A revoked binding cannot recreate a session.

Persist the external identity in `mcp_sessions` so recovery and revocation work across replicas. Materialize it into MCP conversation/activity provenance and event attribution alongside `client_id`.

Likely ownership:

- `packages/server/src/mcp-handler.ts`
- `packages/server/src/mcp-session-store.ts`
- `packages/server/src/tools/execute.ts`
- `packages/server/src/tools/registry.ts`
- `packages/server/src/lobu/stores/mcp-client-conversations.ts`
- Event insertion/attribution surfaces
- MCP integration and recovery tests

Acceptance:

- One call can answer both “who acted?” and “through what?”
- Managed `agentId` binding continues unchanged.
- Wrong-org, wrong-user and wrong-client bindings fail closed.
- Revocation deletes live sessions and makes the profile offline.
- Session recovery on another replica preserves verified actor identity.
- No authorization decision depends on self-asserted vendor/name metadata.

### Phase 4: Give Lobu CLI an explicit actor mode

Keep the CLI itself classified as a Connector:

```text
registered app: Lobu CLI
transport: CLI
actor: absent unless explicitly selected
```

Add an explicit actor selection/declaration flow. The exact command needs approval, but the mechanics should allow:

- Human terminal use with no external agent identity.
- Codex using profile A.
- Claude using profile B.
- CI remaining unclassified or using its own profile.
- Multiple processes against the same Lobu context without overwriting one global actor.

Potential implementation areas:

- `packages/cli/src/internal/oauth.ts`
- `packages/cli/src/internal/credentials.ts`
- `packages/cli/src/internal/context.ts`
- Login/configuration commands
- MCP initialization code
- `whoami` as an additive response change
- `clients` command output

The Mac app shells through Lobu CLI, so the default CLI login must remain actor-less. Otherwise the Mac application could accidentally appear as whichever terminal agent last selected a profile.

Acceptance:

- A plain `lobu login` remains a Lobu CLI Connector only.
- Actor selection is explicit and visible in `whoami`/diagnostics.
- Switching actor profile does not reuse a stale MCP session.
- Credentials are never copied across endpoints, users or workspaces.
- The built CLI is exercised, not only source-level tests.
- The Mac app’s additive `whoami --json` contract remains compatible.

### Phase 5: Build the unified Owletto roster

Once the roster endpoint is stable:

- Replace `useWorkingAgents` with a unified roster hook for sidebar presentation.
- Preserve managed-agent chat links.
- Route external agents to an external-agent detail page.
- Show availability and authorization separately.
- Show transport/vendor details and links back to Connector access management.
- Show capabilities such as “Can claim Behaviors.”
- Show recent actor activity attributed through any bound client.

- Capabilities

- Assigned Behaviors

### Phase 6: Migrate existing data conservatively

Migration principles:

- Preserve all existing OAuth registrations and revocation behavior.
- Old clients default to Connector-only.
- Do not infer historical actor identity from `client_id`; the same client may have represented several actors.
- Historical activity retains transport attribution and an unknown actor.
- Recognized vendors may receive a presentation hint, not verified trust.
- External profiles should be created or bound on the next authenticated declaration or explicit user action.
- Existing current `agentId` MCP bindings remain managed-agent bindings.
- Replace the hard-coded Recent exclusion for `lobu-cli` with semantic transport classification only after coverage is complete.

Acceptance:

- No existing client loses access.
- No historical event is falsely attributed.
- Shared-client revocation remains scoped to the displayed user.
- Old CLIs continue working as Connector-only clients.
- Re-registration does not create duplicate visible actors without an explicit reconciliation path.

## Security test matrix

Server tests should cover:

- Lobu CLI → Connector, not Agent.
- Chrome → Connector, not Agent.
- Mac/CLI-driven Mac → Connector/device, not Agent.
- Generic MCP client → Connector-only.
- Recognized ChatGPT/Claude → catalog hint only.
- A malicious client naming itself “Lobu CLI” or “ChatGPT” gains no trust or scope.
- Self-declared actor metadata cannot bind an unowned profile.
- One registration with Alice and Bob grants cannot cross-bind or cross-revoke.
- Wrong organization/user/client/profile combinations fail.
- Revocation terminates durable and in-memory session state.
- Archived profiles cannot initialize new sessions.
- Session recovery across replicas retains actor binding.
- Managed-agent MCP binding remains unchanged.
- Activity and events contain external actor plus OAuth client attribution.
- Re-registration and refresh-token rotation retain binding safely.
- Unknown/expired/ambiguous rows fail closed.

CLI tests should cover:

- Plain login remains actor-less.
- Selected actor reaches initialize metadata.
- Invalid/stale profile gives actionable output.
- Actor switching forces a fresh session.
- Environment override and stored context cannot accidentally transfer credentials.
- Mac-facing `whoami --json` remains additive.
- Real built-binary invocation.

Owletto tests should cover:

- Only managed/external actor rows under Agents.
- Every app/device/transport still appears in Connectors.
- Correct dual appearance and cross-linking.
- Authorized versus online wording.
- External-agent detail behavior.
- Empty roster CTAs.
- Revocation and archive updates.
- Before/after UI screenshots.

End-to-end trials should exercise:

1. Connect a ChatGPT-like MCP client: Connector appears, no actor yet.
2. Declare/bind an external profile: Agent appears.
3. Reconnect from another replica/process: same actor remains.
4. Use Lobu CLI without actor selection: only “via Lobu CLI” attribution.
5. Use Lobu CLI with a Codex profile: actor is Codex, transport is Lobu CLI.
6. Pair Mac and Chrome: neither becomes an Agent.
7. Revoke a grant: actor stays as a profile but becomes offline/revoked.
8. Reauthorize/re-register: binding is recovered explicitly.
9. Try cross-workspace reuse: rejected.
10. Start with no managed or external agents: onboarding remains functional.
